serpentes.name: Serpentes
serpentes.description: Snakes are a suborder of elongated, limbless, carnivorous reptiles. Their bodies are covered in overlapping scales, and they lack eyelids and external ears. Many species have highly flexible skulls, allowing them to swallow prey much larger than their heads. To accommodate their narrow bodies, paired internal organs like kidneys are arranged one in front of the other, and most possess only one functional lung.

scolecophidia.name: Scolecophidia
scolecophidia.description: Commonly known as blind snakes or thread snakes, this group is adapted for a burrowing (fossorial) lifestyle. They are typically small and worm-like, with smooth, glossy scales and reduced eyes covered by opaque scales. Their diet consists mainly of ants, termites, and their larvae.

alethinophidia.name: Alethinophidia
alethinophidia.description: This infraorder includes all snakes other than the blind snakes. The name means 'true snakes'. This diverse group includes everything from primitive burrowing snakes to the advanced snakes (Caenophidia) with large, flexible jaws capable of consuming large prey.

amerophidia.name: Amerophidia
amerophidia.description: A small, ancient clade of South and Central American snakes representing one of the earliest-diverging lineages of Alethinophidia. Includes the pipe snakes (Anilidae) and dwarf boas (Tropidophiidae). Their position as a sister group to all other true snakes makes them important for understanding early snake evolution.

afrophidia.name: Afrophidia
afrophidia.description: A major clade of Alethinophidia that includes most of the world's snake diversity. It encompasses shield-tail snakes, pipe snakes, pythons, boas, and all advanced snakes. The name reflects their likely African or Gondwanan origin, though the group has since spread to every continent except Antarctica.

uropeltoidea.name: Uropeltoidea
uropeltoidea.description: A superfamily of small, burrowing snakes primarily found in South Asia and Southeast Asia. They include the shield-tail snakes (Uropeltidae), dwarf pipe snakes (Anomochilidae), and Asian pipe snakes (Cylindrophiidae). Many have hardened or keeled tail tips used to plug their burrows against predators.

macrostomata.name: Macrostomata
macrostomata.description: The 'large-mouthed' snakes — a diverse clade defined by highly flexible skulls and jaw ligaments that allow them to swallow prey far larger than their heads. This group includes pythons, boas, and all advanced snakes. The evolution of macrostomate feeding is one of the key innovations in snake evolutionary history.

pythonoidea.name: Pythonoidea
pythonoidea.description: A superfamily of Old World constrictors and their close relatives. Includes the true pythons (Pythonidae), the Mexican burrowing python (Loxocemidae), and the iridescent sunbeam snakes (Xenopeltidae). Pythonoids are egg-layers, distinguishing them from most boas, and some of the largest snakes alive today belong to this group.

booidea.name: Booidea
booidea.description: A superfamily of constricting snakes found across the Americas, Africa, Europe, and the Pacific. What was once classified as a single family (Boidae) is now understood to be several distinct lineages: sand boas (Erycidae), rosy boas and rubber boas (Charinidae), Calabar boa (Calabariidae), Pacific boas (Candoiidae), and Malagasy boas (Sanziniidae). Most are viviparous.

caenophidia.name: Caenophidia
caenophidia.description: Representing over 80% of all living snake species, Caenophidia are the most recently evolved and ecologically diverse snake group. This clade is defined by the loss of a functional left lung and a highly modified skull. It includes the file snakes, vipers, colubrids, elapids, and their relatives. Most of the world's medically important venomous snakes belong here.

colubroides.name: Colubroides
colubroides.description: The largest grouping within Caenophidia, containing the vast majority of all snake species. This clade includes vipers, water snakes, colubrids, and elapids. A defining evolutionary trend is the progressive development of venom delivery systems — from rear-fanged species to the highly derived front-fanged viperid and elapid lineages.

colubroidea.name: Colubroidea
colubroidea.description: A superfamily within Colubroides that contains the largest radiation of snakes on Earth. It includes the colubrids, the lamprophiids (Africa's most diverse snake family), the elapids, and several smaller families. The colubroid lineage represents the peak of snake diversification, occurring mainly in the last 40 million years.

elapoidea.name: Elapoidea
elapoidea.description: A superfamily that includes the most sophisticated venom delivery systems in snakes. Elapoids include cobras, mambas, and sea snakes (Elapidae), Africa's diverse house snakes and their allies (Lamprophiidae), and the stiletto snakes (Atractaspididae). Many species in this group independently evolved fixed front fangs or uniquely specialised fang structures.

colubridae.name: Colubridae
colubridae.description: The largest family of snakes. Most are harmless to humans and are typically non-venomous or have mild, rear-fanged venom. They are found worldwide in nearly every habitat. Due to its diversity, it was historically a 'wastebasket' taxon for snakes that didn't fit elsewhere.

elapidae.name: Elapidae
elapidae.description: A family of highly venomous snakes with fixed, hollow fangs at the front of the mouth (proteroglyphous). The venom is typically neurotoxic. This family includes cobras, mambas, coral snakes, and sea snakes. They have slender bodies and are found in tropical and subtropical regions around the world.

viperidae.name: Viperidae
viperidae.description: A family of venomous snakes with long, hollow, hinged fangs that fold back against the roof of the mouth (solenoglyphous). They typically have stocky bodies, a distinct triangular head, and vertically elliptical pupils. Most are nocturnal ambush predators. This family includes vipers, rattlesnakes, and adders.

boidae.name: Boidae
boidae.description: A family of non-venomous constrictors, including some of the world's largest snakes like the anaconda. They are primarily found in the Americas. Most give birth to live young (viviparous) and have heat-sensing pits along their lips to detect warm-blooded prey. They retain vestigial hind limbs as 'spurs'.

pythonidae.name: Pythonidae
pythonidae.description: A family of non-venomous constrictors found in the Old World (Africa, Asia, Australia). Unlike boas, they lay eggs (oviparous) and some species exhibit maternal care by coiling around their eggs to incubate them. They also possess heat-sensing pits. Most have teeth on the premaxilla.

atractaspididae.name: Atractaspididae
atractaspididae.description: A family of venomous snakes found in Africa and the Middle East, commonly known as stiletto snakes, mole vipers, or burrowing asps. They possess a unique fang structure and venom delivery system that allows them to stab prey sideways with their mouth closed, an adaptation for hunting in narrow burrows. Their venom can cause severe local tissue damage and, in some species, is cardiotoxic.

typhlopidae.name: Typhlopidae
typhlopidae.description: A family of blind snakes found in most tropical and subtropical regions. They are fossorial (burrowing) snakes with cylindrical bodies, smooth scales, and vestigial eyes that can only detect light. They are often mistaken for earthworms. Their diet consists primarily of the eggs, larvae, and pupae of ants and termites.

leptotyphlopidae.name: Leptotyphlopidae
leptotyphlopidae.description: Known as thread snakes or slender blind snakes, this family contains some of the smallest snakes in the world. The Barbados threadsnake (Tetracheilostoma carlae) holds the record for the world's smallest snake, reaching only about 10 cm. Like other blind snakes, they live underground and feed on ant and termite colonies.

tropidophiidae.name: Tropidophiidae
tropidophiidae.description: The dwarf boas of the Caribbean and South America. These small to medium constrictors are known for an unusual and dramatic defensive behavior: when threatened, some species can rupture blood vessels around their eyes and mouth, bleeding from their face to deter predators. They are viviparous and share several anatomical features with the ancient boa lineage.

xenopeltidae.name: Xenopeltidae
xenopeltidae.description: The sunbeam snakes of Southeast Asia are renowned for their extraordinary iridescent scales, which produce a brilliant rainbow sheen in sunlight due to microstructured scale surfaces that diffract light. Despite this flashy appearance, they are secretive, burrowing snakes. Their skull anatomy is considered intermediate between primitive and advanced snakes, making them scientifically important.

acrochordidae.name: Acrochordidae
acrochordidae.description: The file snakes (or wart snakes) are among the most specialised aquatic snakes on Earth. They are completely aquatic, never leaving the water voluntarily, and their loose, baggy skin covered in tiny granular scales gives them their sandpaper-like texture. They lack the ventral scales used for locomotion on land. Found in coastal waters, estuaries, and rivers across South and Southeast Asia.

homalopsidae.name: Homalopsidae
homalopsidae.description: A family of rear-fanged, semi-aquatic to fully aquatic snakes found across South and Southeast Asia. Most are associated with freshwater and brackish environments. Dog-faced water snakes and mudsnakes belong here. Though rear-fanged, most are not considered dangerous to humans. Several species are notable for foraging in mudflats and tidal zones.

lamprophiidae.name: Lamprophiidae
lamprophiidae.description: Africa's most diverse snake family, with over 300 species spread across sub-Saharan Africa and Madagascar. This family includes the stiletto snakes (formerly Atractaspididae), house snakes, wolf snakes, and many others. Lamprophiids occupy a huge range of ecological niches — burrowing, semi-aquatic, arboreal — and range from completely harmless to dangerously venomous.
